newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta to stop plans for privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Malta to stop plans for privatisation.

text.p: Malta's new Labour government is to stop plans by the previous administration partly or wholly to privatise state companies, Finance Minister Lino Spiteri said.

"We are saying we shall not sell them, they are a source of revenue for us, but this is tied to a commitment that such companies shall operate commercially" the minister told Reuters in a recent interview.
The former Nationalist government had privatised Bank of Valletta, Malta's second largest bank, the tiny Lombard Bank (Malta) and a handful of small firms.
It had also announced its intention to issue shares in Mid-Med Bank, Air Malta and Gozo Channel, the ferry line that links Malta with the sister island of Gozo.
Spiteri said government stock would continue to be traded on the stock exchange. Only five companies are listed so far -- three banks, an insurance company and a soft drinks maker.

"I hope that in due time the private sector will come forward...it is a decision which it has to take, but the stock exchange mechanism is there for the whole economy and it would be wrong to assume that its continuing existence is dependent on privatisation of government entities," he said.

The share issue and a strong Labour commitment to remove Value Added Tax are the only major changes the new government intends to make from the previous government's economic and financial policies. The Maltese economy grew by an average five percent annually in the past few years.
Spiteri said the government-nominated Governor of the Central Bank would stay on, as would the chairmen of the Malta Financial Services Centre and the Malta Stock Exchange.

He reiterated Labour's commitment to repeal VAT, brought in by the previous government as it geared up for membership of the European Union. Labour is against EU membership, arguing that several EU regulations are unsuitable for Malta.
Prime Minister Alfred Sant has said Malta's application, submitted in 1990, will not be formally withdrawn. He says the removal of VAT shows Malta does not want full membership.
The Malta Federation of Industry said on Monday this could cause uncertainty over the EU and harm investment. But Spiteri insisted there was no uncertainty.
"Uncertainty should have eased, not worsened since the election, as the new government's policy on Europe is clear, we want the closest possible ties short of membership."
Spiteri said the government did not intend introducing higher taxes but it would wage a fight on tax evasion.
"We shall not reintroduce high tax rates. The existing tax regime is reasonable. Within it one should be able to operate in a just manner and I am encouraging people to do so."
Nor would the government change conditions on financial operations. "We have a good set of legislation in place, so we should be able to work within it," he said.
The government aimed at total liberalisation of exchange control but would pace it according to the economy.

Spiteri, a former Central Bank deputy governor, said efforts to attract foreign banks to Malta would be kept up. Six banks have been licensed to operate offshore. The British-based Midland Bank is the only foreign bank granted a full licence, last year, to provide banking services in Malta.
Spiteri said: "We shall continue to promote the island as a serious base from which financial services can be profitably provided, not just for the domestic market...but even beyond."
